body:
To give some context, this is the result of a discussion I've had with SCons maintainers (one of which is the OP) about our current performance with cached non-incremental ninja builds.

To put it in the simplest terms possible, scons tries its best to translate its build graph into native ninja commands, with a fallback to a direct scons invocation for tricker files. Due to the (discouraged) way we generated `*.gen.*` files, they *all* fell back to scons, with serious performance issues.

It doesn't help that this scons fallback thing is single-threaded and we have such chonky generator methods that it wasn't rare to see ninja timing out when trying to build multiple things. A workaround I've found is to disable ninja autorun, then call `ninja -j1 run-ninja-scons-daemon` and only then do a plain `ninja` call. I *think* that it's a bug that it doesn't keep scons invocations into a single-threaded pool, but I haven't investigated this issue yet.

This PR allows scons to translate all custom generators into ninja commands, giving it control of pretty much the whole build graph. This turns ninja times competitive, if not superior, to plain scons.

As per #118796, this considerably speeds up my use-case (custom build container for testing builds).

Results follow.

First of all, the usual stuff: completely cached builds with scons cache and ninja + ccache, before and after. This includes one warmup run per benchmark and two "build" runs, which cover the whole build container lifecycle: container bringup, updating git, building a tarball, only then "building" the engine, plus cleanup.

The conditions are the same as in the benchmarks for #118796. Forced clock, turbo off, performance governor, etc.

Please note that the following still forces single-threaded generation for ninja even in the case of this PR (I forgor :skull:)

<details>

```
Benchmark 1: master (scons cache)
  Time (mean ± σ):     149.608 s ±  7.403 s    [User: 23.867 s, System: 6.071 s]
  Range (min … max):   144.374 s … 154.843 s    2 runs
 
Benchmark 2: master (ninja + ccache)
  Time (mean ± σ):     170.320 s ±  1.346 s    [User: 23.890 s, System: 6.171 s]
  Range (min … max):   169.368 s … 171.272 s    2 runs
 
Benchmark 3: Actions to command (scons cache)
  Time (mean ± σ):     144.739 s ±  2.415 s    [User: 25.049 s, System: 6.242 s]
  Range (min … max):   143.032 s … 146.447 s    2 runs
 
Benchmark 4: Actions to command (ninja + ccache)
  Time (mean ± σ):     151.175 s ±  4.449 s    [User: 23.957 s, System: 6.195 s]
  Range (min … max):   148.029 s … 154.321 s    2 runs
 
Summary
  Actions to command (scons cache) ran
    1.03 ± 0.05 times faster than master (scons cache)
    1.04 ± 0.04 times faster than Actions to command (ninja + ccache)
    1.18 ± 0.02 times faster than master (ninja + ccache)
```

</details>

`master` was e06dd8106e4c9113f2a3b20e4ceef16f3e85735e, onto which the branch I tested built on (up to "Fixed ruff format").

It's already pretty good if you ask me. I think most of the ninja time save in this PR is the fact that it doesn't have to invoke scons anymore.

Ninja is now vastly comparable, although scons got a nice boost too. I think that's because the generated files are now part of the scons cache, which wasn't the case before.

Now, after I figured out my mistake of leaving the single-threaded hack, here comes the kicker:

```
Benchmark 1: Actions to command (ninja + ccache, no pre-gen step)
  Time (mean ± σ):     100.349 s ±  1.378 s    [User: 24.020 s, System: 6.165 s]
  Range (min … max):   99.375 s … 101.324 s    2 runs
```

That's *fast*. To make sure it wasn't a fluke and I forgot to set the clock correctly, I also tried by turning turbo on (which is double the clock) and got roughly half the times. This to me looks like the full potential of ninja!

Edit: I must add that my tests had to workaround a bug where some runtime files self-deleted before ninja could invoke them. I'm not sure if this has been fixed yet, but in case I attach a workaround. This will not clean them up anymore, which are placed in `<godot dir>/.ninja/.response_files`

<details>

<summary>Workaround patch</summary>

```diff
--- a/site_scons/site_tools/handle_long_lines.py
+++ b/site_scons/site_tools/handle_long_lines.py
@@ -5,7 +5,6 @@ are excepted from being included in the generated response file if the command l
 long for the OS's shell
 """
 
-import atexit
 import contextlib
 import os
 import sys
@@ -164,7 +163,7 @@ class MyTempFileMunge:
             with contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError):
                 os.remove(file)
 
-        atexit.register(tmpfile_cleanup, tmp)
+        # atexit.register(tmpfile_cleanup, tmp)
 
         # XXX Using the SCons.Action.print_actions value directly
         # like this is bogus, but expedient.  This class should
```

@deralmas - I've pushed an update which changes MYTEMPFILE to not register atexit temp file deletion logic if you're doing a ninja build.  Also added MYTEMPFILE around one of the already migrated actions as it was exceeding line length during ninja build for 
`py -3 C:\devel\scons\git\as_scons\scripts\scons.py platform=windows target=editor ninja=yes`

@bdbaddog tested the change, it works now, thank you! I can see that the lnk files don't get deleted between generations. I recall you talking about a cleaning action on Discord, did you get to try that?

I also did lots of tinkering with the benchmark thing in the past few days and realized that there's a lot of noise. I had *a lot* of trouble getting consistent results. Relative speedups would stay roughly consistent (e.g. `t(ninja) < t(plain scons)`) but the factors would change randomly (e.g ninja was 1.12 to 1.52 times faster than plain scons depending on the environment). I gutted the build script to the bare minimum and even then I would have issues, which most notably manifested as SSD churn.

My conclusion given the above is I/O, confirmed by using `tmpfs`, which gave the least deviation and highest results. That makes sense, as most operations in this case are (hopefully) copying from cache into the working dir. It looks like it makes fresh static archives all the time too, I think that also eats a lot of I/O.

---

The following is my best attempt to date at reducing all noise. In a way, this is the closest thing I could do to a synthetic test with my knowledge and time.

Setup: `amd-pstate` set to `passive`, `userspace` governor, 2.00GHz clock, no copy of the resulting binary to persistent storage, no network fetching (I always test without Wi-Fi so it would just timeout), `tmpfs` working volume, host filesystem is now XFS. 1 warmup run, 4 runs.

<details>

<summary>"Clean" builds, fully cached by scons/ccache (please take this with a grain of salt)</summary>

```
Benchmark 1: master (e06dd8106e) (scons cache) 
  Time (mean ± σ):     99.266 s ±  1.326 s    [User: 24.210 s, System: 3.458 s]
  Range (min … max):   98.038 s … 100.644 s    4 runs
 
Benchmark 2: Actions to command (scons cache)
  Time (mean ± σ):     83.961 s ±  0.860 s    [User: 24.229 s, System: 3.459 s]
  Range (min … max):   82.911 s … 84.999 s    4 runs
 
Benchmark 3: master (e06dd8106e) (ninja + ccache, pregen)
  Time (mean ± σ):     119.312 s ±  0.560 s    [User: 23.593 s, System: 3.389 s]
  Range (min … max):   118.541 s … 119.831 s    4 runs
 
Benchmark 4: Actions to command (ninja + ccache, pregen)
  Time (mean ± σ):     92.290 s ±  0.704 s    [User: 23.986 s, System: 3.449 s]
  Range (min … max):   91.889 s … 93.340 s    4 runs
 
  Warning: Statistical outliers were detected. Consider re-running this benchmark on a quiet system without any interferences from other programs. It might help to use the '--warmup' or '--prepare' options.
 
Benchmark 5: Actions to command (ninja + ccache, no pregen)
  Time (mean ± σ):     65.133 s ±  0.549 s    [User: 23.432 s, System: 3.334 s]
  Range (min … max):   64.676 s … 65.921 s    4 runs
 
Summary
  Actions to command (ninja + ccache, no pregen) ran
    1.29 ± 0.02 times faster than Actions to command (scons cache)
    1.42 ± 0.02 times faster than Actions to command (ninja + ccache, pregen)
    1.52 ± 0.02 times faster than master (e06dd8106e) (scons cache)
    1.83 ± 0.02 times faster than master (e06dd8106e) (ninja + ccache, pregen)
```

</details>

No idea why it talks about statistical outliers tbh, my laptop had pretty much nothing running outside of sway. Another reason to take this with a grain of salt :P

---

I could play with this for a while but I guess the real point of it is that it has been consistently faster to use ninja with this branch, so at least we can validate that claim. Maybe we could also conclude that this is heavily I/O bound and that ninja + ccache can use it better but I'm not sure if that's really a surprise xD

For everything else, I would really not take these results too seriously, as this is both an extreme case (cached clean build) and setup (building in RAM). Undoubtedly this makes general QoL better as the `Defer to SCons to build...` part was so slow and it would actively timeout during normal development, but we didn't really need the above to know that :D

That said I feel like this was an interesting experiment and hope that it might shine some light into the potential of this stuff, if any of it is actually reproducible.

Talking about reproducible, if anyone wants to experiment with the same scripts I got, feel free to ask! I'm not sure if I'll ever publish them as-is since they're so hacky but I don't mind making a zip or something with some instructions if anyone's interested. They're based on the [official build scripts](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-build-scripts.git) and [containers](https://github.com/godotengine/build-containers).

I tried to compile this branch as-is and **failed** (it resulted in something about a harfbuzz API fail).
Assuming that was a general bug, I also tried rebasing on top of latest master and that one compiled, so after a rebase it should be working just fine.

I'm not sure what else I'm meant to test but I can confirm that scons tries very hard to be reproducible (I know because I'm on NixOS and the two reproducibility paradigms really don't get along). It will clear all env vars except PATH and PKG_CONFIG_PATH (at least on Linux) before executing ninja so as long as you have those two under control you should be fine.
